Detailed Office Action
The communication dated 2/24/2023 has been entered and fully considered.
Claims 1-18 are pending.
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 9 and 10 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Regarding claims 9 and 10, the phrase preferably renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitation(s) following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.  See MPEP § 2173.05(d).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
Claims 1-18 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over EP 3059344 A1 ANTILLA et al., hereinafter ANTILLA, in view of WO 2020/084188 A1 ANTILLA, hereinafter ANTILLA II.
As for claims 1 and 2, ANTILLA discloses supercalendering of glassine paper [0051].  The Examiner notes that the intended use of the paper in the preamble is non-limiting, nevertheless, ANTILLA discloses that the glassine paper is suitable for a release liner [0051].  ANTILLA discloses that the paper comprises both bleached hardwood and softwood chemical pulps [0077] and those chemical pulps can be kraft chemical pulps [0058] (A supercalendered kraft paper suitable for use as a substrate layer of an industrial release liner for adhesive labels, the supercalendered kraft paper comprising).
ANTILLA discloses a basis weight of 57 g/m2 [0077] which falls within the claimed range (a basis weight in the range of 50 to 70 g/m2, when determined according to ISO 536).
ANTILLA discloses that the furnish comprises, bleached chemical hardwood, bleached chemical softwood and bleached CTMP pulp [0077] (fiber furnish determinable with standard ISO 9184-4 in conjunction with standard ISO 9184-1, the fiber furnish comprising of bleached hardwood kraft pulp, of bleached softwood kraft pulp and of bleached chemithermomechanical pulp)
ANTILLA discloses 25% bleached CTMP which falls within the claimed range [0077] (such that the supercalendered kraft paper contains - the bleached chemithermomechanical pulp in an amount equal to or higher than 5 wt.%).
ANTILLA discloses a transparency of 46.5% which falls within the claimed range [0078] (the supercalendered kraft paper thereby having - a transparency level equal to or higher than 40%, when determined according to ISO 2469).
ANTILLA discloses a density of 1087 kg/m2 which falls within the claimed range [0077] (a density in the range of 1040 to 1140 kg/m3, when determined according to ISO 534).
ANTILLA discloses a mixture of bleached softwood and hardwood kraft chemical pulps.  ANTILLA does not disclose the specific amount of hardwood and softwood.  However, ANTILLA recognizes that the split of hardwood and softwood is a result effective variable.  ANTILLA discloses that hardwood fibers provide greater brightness which increases transparency [0029, 0033] while softwood fibers provide greater strength properties.  At the time of the invention it would be obvious to the person of ordinary skill in the art to optimize the amount of hardwood and softwood kraft chemical fibers through routine optimization to achieve a balance between strength and brightness/transparency (the bleached softwood kraft pulp in an amount equal to or higher than 15 wt.%, when determined as dry matter content of the paper according to SCAN-P 39:80).
Furthermore, the Examiner notes that differences in concentration will not typically support non-obviousness absent evidence of unexpected results.
In the alternative, if necessary, ANTILLA II discloses release papers which comprise bleached kraft chemical pulps [pg. 32 lines 5-10].  ANTILLA II discloses that hardwood fibers provide brightness and transparency while softwood fibers provide strength [pg. 30 lines 5-20].  ANTILLA II discloses a split of fibers of 10-35% which overlaps with the instant claimed range [pg. 31 lines 5-9].
At the time of the invention it would be obvious to the person of ordinary skill in the art to apply the known concentration of hardwood and softwood chemical kraft pulps for release liner of ANILLA II to the chemical pulp concentrations of ANTILLA.  The person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated to do so to achieve the desired balance between the properties offered by hardwoods and softwoods.
As for claim 3, ANTILLA discloses that the bleached CTMP may have an SR of 25 to 55 [0058] which falls within the claimed range.
As for claim 4 and 5, as ANTILLA and if necessary, ANTILLA II, teach the substantially the same fiber composition (kraft hardwood, kraft softwood, BCTMP) at substantially the same degree of refining (SR) for the backing later of a release liner it would be expected to have substantially the same length weighted average fiber length and average fiber width.  Fiber length and fiber width are dependent on the type of fibers used and the degree of refining (SR value).  Alternatively, fiber type (hardwood (short fibers) vs softwood (long fibers)) is a result effective variable (see supra).  At the time of the invention it would be obvious to optimize the proportion of hardwood and softwood and therefore the average fiber length/width through routine optimization.
As for claim 6, ANTILLA discloses 25% bleached CTMP which falls within the claimed range [0077].
As for claim 7, ANTILLA discloses 25% bleached CTMP which falls within the claimed range [0077]
As for claims 8 and 9, ANTILLA discloses that the bleached CTMP comprises both hardwood and softwood fibers [0077].  ANTILLA discloses the hardwood aspen (genus populus) and the softwood spruce (genus Picea) [0076].
As for claim 10, ANTILLA discloses that the softwood can be present in the mixture of hardwood and softwood bleached CTMP of 10 to 35% which falls within the claimed range [0112].
As for claim 11, ANTILLA discloses a basis weight of 57 g/m2 [0077] which falls within the claimed range.
As for claim 12, ANTILLA discloses a transparency of 46.5% which falls within the claimed range [0078].
As for claim 13, ANTILLA discloses bleached kraft chemical pulp and bleached CTMP pulp for the release liner paper.  ANTILLA does not disclose how bright the paper should be ANTILLA II discloses a lightness (L*) of at least 94% which overlaps the instant claimed range, an a* of -5 to 1 which overlaps the instant claimed range and a b* of 4 to 10 which overlaps the instant claimed range [pg. 41 lines 20-30].    At the time of the invention it would be obvious to the person of ordinary skill in the art to apply the known CIE L*a*b* values of ANTILLA II to the release liner of ANTILLA.  The person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated to do so to improve the product by increasing the market are at which it is sold [ANTILLA II pg.41 lines 30-35].  The person of ordinary skill in the art would expect success as ANTILLA states that release papers should be bleached such that they have whiteness and brightness [0028].
As for claim 14, ANTILLA discloses a density of 1087 kg/m2 which falls within the claimed range [0077].
As for claims 15 and 17, as ANTILLA teaches substantially the same furnish composition and substantially the same degree of refining it would be expected the furnish would have substantially the same water retention value and tear index.  The properties of a composition cannot be separated from the composition itself.
As for claim 16, ANTILLA discloses an example of paper with 35% bleached CTMP and the remainder of chemical pulp [0089].
ANTILLA discloses a mixture of bleached softwood and hardwood kraft chemical pulps.  ANTILLA does not disclose the specific amount of hardwood and softwood.  However, ANTILLA recognizes that the split of hardwood and softwood is a result effective variable.  ANTILLA discloses that hardwood fibers provide greater brightness which increases transparency [0029, 0033] while softwood fibers provide greater strength properties.  At the time of the invention it would be obvious to the person of ordinary skill in the art to optimize the amount of hardwood and softwood kraft chemical fibers through routine optimization to achieve a balance between strength and transparency (the bleached softwood kraft pulp in an amount equal to or higher than 15 wt.%, when determined as dry matter content of the paper according to SCAN-P 39:80).
Furthermore, the Examiner notes that differences in concentration will not typically support non-obviousness absent evidence of unexpected results.
In the alternative, if necessary, ANTILLA II discloses release papers which comprise bleached kraft chemical pulps [pg. 32 lines 5-10].  ANTILLA II discloses that hardwood fibers provide brightness and transparency while softwood fibers provide strength [pg. 30 lines 5-20].  ANTILLA II discloses a split of fibers of 10-35% which overlaps with the instant claimed range [pg. 31 lines 5-9].  With 35% BTCMP and 10-35% softwood this leaves 30-55% bleached chemical hardwood which overlaps the instant claimed range
At the time of the invention it would be obvious to the person of ordinary skill in the art to apply the known concentration of hardwood and softwood chemical kraft pulps for release liner of ANILLA II to the chemical pulp concentrations of ANTILLA.  The person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated to do so to achieve the desired balance between the properties offered by hardwoods and softwoods.
As for claim 18, ANTILLA discloses a release coating on the supercalendered paper [0002].
Conclusion
